sourceSpan.excerpt: In raising the question of God's existence, we are in effect engaging in the assessment of a metaphysical hypothesis, namely the hypothesis that God exists. Accordingly, we need to ask ourselves two questions with respect to this hypothesis: first, what evidence is there that serves to falsify this hypothesis? And second, what evidence is there that serves to verify this hypothesis? Now with respect to the first question, I'll leave it up to Dr. Piliucci to present the reasons why he thinks that this hypothesis is false. Atheists have tried for centuries to disprove the existence of God, but no one has been able to come up with a successful argument. Dr. Pilieucci, on the other hand, in his article God as a Falsifiable Hypothesis says my position is that belief in God can be falsified. So rather than attack straw men at this point, I'll just wait to hear Dr. Pilieucci's answer to the following question: What good evidence is there to falsify the hypothesis that God exists? Let's look then instead at the second question, what evidence is there that serves to verify God's existence? And tonight I'm going to present five pieces of evidence in support of the specific hypothesis that a creator and designer of the universe exists, who is the locus of absolute value and who has revealed himself in Jesus Christ.

moves.description: Craig defines the Christian God through several attributes and proposes five mutually reinforcing considerations intended to make that specific hypothesis the best overall explanation.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig clearly defines the affirmative hypothesis and announces a cumulative method, allowing each later consideration to be evaluated both independently and for its contribution toward the specifically Christian conclusion. Principal limitation: The opening architecture does not itself show that cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, resurrection, and experience converge on one agent rather than supporting different, weaker, or merely generic hypotheses. Live burden: He must establish each bridge without treating unexplained phenomena as automatically theistic, then explain how the resurrection component supplies the Christian specificity missing from the earlier considerations.

moves.speaker: Massimo Pigliucci

moves.warrant: Pigliucci distinguishes the specific Christian motion from generic concepts of God and states a critical, evidence-focused posture.
moves.inference: Evidence that at most supports an unspecified deity does not by itself discharge the exact motion.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Well, thanks everybody for coming, and especially to the organizers for organizing this lively debate. I hope that we're all going to be learning something tonight from it. As Dr. Craig said, I will examine these five arguments in sequence, and I will try to make a point that they're actually not that convincing. In fact, they're not convincing at all. And then we'll get probably during the rebuttal time to what kind of positive arguments are possible or even needed on the other side of the debate. So my basic thesis is this. While I don't know the truth, and neither does Dr. Craig, neither of us really know what's going on here, it is beyond reasonable doubt, I think, that the Christian God is the result of the human imagination. Notice that I'm talking about the Christian God in particular. and not of any concept of God. Dr. Craig spent quite a bit of time talking about generalized versions of God. This was not the topic of the debate, but I knew he was going to do that.

moves.description: Pigliucci argues that generic arguments for a creator do not establish Christianity and demands evidence distinguishing the Christian God from other divine hypotheses.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci accurately identifies a decisive scope issue: cosmological, design, and moral arguments can at most support broad theism unless additional premises connect their conclusion to Christianity’s historical and doctrinal claims. Principal limitation: He sometimes treats imperfect specificity as total irrelevance, although generic theistic evidence could legitimately raise the prior plausibility of a later Christian-specific resurrection argument within a cumulative case. Live burden: His critical task is to expose missing bridges and rival compatibility, while any positive claim that the generic evidence has no cumulative relevance requires more than observing that it is not uniquely Christian.

moves.inference: The general arguments need not individually prove Christianity if they narrow the hypothesis cumulatively before the resurrection step.

sourceSpan.excerpt: You'll recall that in my opening speech I proposed a specific hypothesis that a personal creator and designer of the universe exists who is the locus of absolute value and has revealed himself in Jesus Christ. Now, I'm astonished that Dr. Piliucci has yielded all but the last point. He admits in tonight's debate that the arguments for personal creator and designer of the universe are sound and he's willing to even grant that he is the locus of absolute value. So the whole debate comes down to whether or not this person has revealed himself in Jesus Christ. Now, that's astonishing when you think about it because already those first three arguments for a creator and designer of the universe narrow down the field of the world's religions to Judaism, Islam, and Christianity. so that you've already narrowed it down to those three. And the real question then is the resurrection of Jesus. Now what's surprising about this is that this is the one area in which Dr. Piliucci as an evolutionary biologist is the least expert to speak on. And yet this is where he's chosen to stake his camp tonight. So we'll have to see whether or not in fact he can defend that. Now you remember I said there were two questions we need to assess tonight. What is the evidence that falsifies my hypothesis? And second, what is the evidence that verifies it? We've heard no evidence tonight to suggest that the God hypothesis is false. He simply tried to refute my evidence in verification of the hypothesis. So at best we're left with neutrality. The only question is then whether or not we have good reasons to verify that hypothesis.

moves.description: Craig replies that generic theistic arguments combine with resurrection evidence to reach Christianity and argues that Pigliucci’s claimed neutrality carries its own assumptions.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig directly explains the intended routing of his case: broad arguments establish a theistic context, and the resurrection then functions as the discriminator for the Christian conclusion. Principal limitation: Restating cumulative architecture does not establish that the components are probabilistically independent or mutually reinforcing, and describing criticism as nonneutral risks shifting attention from the affirmative’s evidential burden. Live burden: Craig must show how much each generic argument contributes and why resurrection selects Christianity among live rivals, rather than requiring Pigliucci to justify a complete atheistic worldview before criticizing those links.

sourceSpan.excerpt: OK, he says that I have not provided any way to falsify the belief in God, or in the Christian God in particular, which, remember, was the topic for tonight. I'm not sure what he means in terms of falsification. I know what the term means as applied to science and empirical evidence. As applied to stories about supernatural beings, it's much less clear. He's fond of quoting that article that I wrote for Skeptic magazine a few years ago, saying that he quotes me as saying that you can falsify the existence of God. That's not really what I said. If you had read, actually, the whole article, you would find that I was saying that you can falsify certain specific claims about the physicality of the universe, which are found in biblical or other sacred texts. For example, you can falsify that there was or was not a Noah's flood, or things of that sort. But not the metaphysical claim of the existence of any god. So I'm not sure where he got that one. However, the question I'd like to ask you is, do you need a positive argument not to believe in, say, leprechauns or Santa Claus? Or do I just need to make an argument that whatever reason you provide me for believing in Santa Claus can be debunked pretty easily? You say, hey, I found the toys under the tree last Christmas. Yes, but there is such a thing as a toy industry. And actually, your father has a credit card. And here is the statement. It shows on your credit card on your father's credit card. So that's a pretty good explanation of a piece of empirical evidence. Do I really need to demonstrate that there is no Santa Claus? No, of course I cannot demonstrate that there is no Santa Claus. You cannot demonstrate that there is anything, things that you cannot touch, you cannot see. They don't have any effect on the physical world outside of what Dr. Craig was saying. So I don't think that the falsifiability argument is very strong, in fact, strong at all.

moves.description: Pigliucci argues that broad God claims evade falsification and clarifies that rejecting insufficient evidence does not obligate him to prove metaphysical impossibility.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci carefully separates lack of belief from the stronger assertion that no God could exist, protecting a limited critical burden and highlighting how elastic divine hypotheses can absorb contrary observations. Principal limitation: Falsifiability is not the sole criterion for rational metaphysical inference, and Pigliucci’s own stronger remarks about miracles, natural explanation, and irrelevance sometimes go beyond simple evidential suspension. Live burden: He need not prove universal nonexistence to challenge Craig’s case, but he must support any positive claims he adopts and specify what expected evidence would count against the Christian hypothesis.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig

sourceSpan.excerpt: I think it's remarkable that in tonight's debate we have still yet to hear any evidence to falsify the God hypothesis. In his last speech, Dr. Piliucci said, we don't have to have a positive argument to believe that God doesn't exist. Look at Santa Claus, we don't need a positive argument not to believe in him. I would submit, on the contrary, any time you make a claim that something doesn't exist, that is a claim to knowledge and therefore you have a burden of proof to justify it. Scott Shalkowski, in his article in the American Philosophical Quarterly of 1989, makes this point very well. He says, the reason adults disbelieve in Santa Claus is not simply that there is no good reason to think that he exists, but because we have good reasons to think that he does not. So Dr. Piliucci similarly needs to give us good reasons to think that God does not exist. Shalkowski concludes, there is no good reason for the presumption of atheism that is prevalent in many Western intellectual circles. I have been unable to find a good argument which places differential burdens of proof on theists and atheists. There is no justification for the current atheistic rage in the absence of atheological apologetics. The absence of such apologetics is quite striking, and it's certainly been striking in tonight's debate.

moves.description: Craig argues that asserted divine nonexistence requires positive reasons, using adult disbelief in Santa to distinguish justified denial from mere absence of belief.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig clearly distinguishes withholding belief from asserting nonexistence and explains that adult disbelief in Santa rests on positive counterevidence rather than a bare absence of support. Principal limitation: The argument does not establish equal burdens for every negative existential claim, and Pigliucci’s debate posture is often critical nonbelief rather than the universal denial Craig broadly attributes to him. Live burden: Craig may demand justification for con’s explicit knowledge claims without transferring his own affirmative obligation to establish the Christian God.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Okay, a few more random points in sequence that have been presented by Dr. Craig. I won't get to reject, to refute all of them. Rejecting the existence of something for which there is no reason to believe is an entirely rational thing to do, and you do it every single day. You don't believe in leprechauns, you don't believe, most of you, don't believe in unicorns, you don't believe in the fact that there are invisible people that hold together this table and don't let it fall apart, and all sorts of other beliefs you just don't have those beliefs. On the other hand, you cannot prove that there are no leprechauns. You cannot prove that there are no unicorns. You cannot prove that there are no invisible people around here that are holding this table together. Why don't you believe it? Because it's very rational and it's very, very, very logical not to believe things for which there is no evidence if those things require extraordinary leaps of faith, if they violate basic laws of physics and biology, with which we're all familiar.

moves.description: Pigliucci argues that rational nonbelief follows from inadequate evidence and does not require proving God impossible, much as people reject unsupported extraordinary entities.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci states the evidential burden with useful precision: a person may rationally withhold belief when support is insufficient without assuming the heavier task of demonstrating logical impossibility. Principal limitation: Analogies with leprechauns or other entities work only if the expected evidence and background knowledge are relevantly similar, and they can bypass Craig’s positive cumulative arguments rather than evaluate them. Live burden: Pigliucci must show why the offered evidence fails or why the Christian hypothesis predicts observations not found, while supporting only those stronger nonexistence claims he actually makes.

sourceSpan.excerpt: In my closing speech, I'd like to draw together the threads of the debate and give some assessment of the arguments. First, have we seen any reasons tonight to falsify the God hypothesis? I think the answer is clearly no. Dr. Piliucci simply says that we reject things due to the absence of evidence, not always, only sometime. For example, if we were to say, is there an elephant in this room? The absence of any evidence would be a good reason to think there is no elephant in this room. But if someone were to assert there is no flea in this room, would the absence of evidence for the flea be a good reason to think there's not a flea in the room? Well, clearly not. The point is that absence of evidence is evidence of absence only in the case where if the thing did exist, you would expect to have some more evidence of it than what you do. And in the case of God, Dr. Piliucci simply hasn't shown us that if God did exist, that we would expect to have more evidence than such as I've laid out tonight. He says, well, what about other things like leprechauns? They violate the laws of physics and biology. Exactly, that's my point. You have positive reasons to not believe that those things exist. But in the case of God, this doesn't violate the laws of physics and biology. We've had no good reason tonight to think that the God hypothesis is false. On the contrary, any evidence that's been given tonight has been on the side of

moves.description: Craig argues that absent evidence supports absence only when a hypothesis predicts detectable evidence that is missing, a condition Pigliucci has not established for God.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig’s elephant-and-flea contrast clearly states the expectation principle governing negative evidence and directly reveals what is missing from a bare appeal to nondetection. Principal limitation: He does not specify what the Christian God hypothesis predicts we should observe, so the principle can insulate a flexible hypothesis unless divine purposes and expected evidence are independently constrained. Live burden: Craig retains the duty to establish his positive cumulative case and articulate relevant predictions; Pigliucci must identify reasonably expected evidence that is absent rather than rely on generic invisibility analogies.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The number of past events in the history of the universe is infinite, but mathematicians recognize that the existence of an actually infinite number of things leads to self-contradictions. For example, what is infinity minus infinity? Well, mathematically you get self-contradictory answers. This shows that infinity is just an idea in your mind, not something that exists in reality. David Hilbert, who was perhaps the greatest mathematician of the 20th century, states, the infinite is nowhere to be found in reality. It neither exists in nature nor provides a legitimate basis for rational thought. The role that remains for the infinite to play is solely that of an idea. But that entails that since past events are not just ideas but are real, that the number of past events must be finite. Therefore the series of past events can't just go back forever, rather the universe must have begun to exist. This conclusion has been confirmed by remarkable discoveries in astronomy and astrophysics. The astrophysical evidence indicates that the universe began to exist in a cataclysmic explosion called the Big Bang about 15 billion years ago. Natural space and time were created in that event, as well as all the matter and energy in the universe. Therefore as the Cambridge astronomer Fred Hoyle points out, the Big Bang theory requires the creation of the universe from nothing. This is because as you go back in time, you reach a point at which, in Hoyle's words, the universe was shrunk down to nothing at all. Because what the Big Bang model requires is that the universe began to exist and was created out of nothing. Now this tends to be very awkward for the atheist, for as Anthony Kinney of Oxford University urges, a proponent of the Big Bang theory, at least if he is an atheist, must believe that the universe came from nothing and by nothing. But surely that doesn't make sense. Out of nothing, nothing comes. So why does the universe exist instead of just nothing? Where did it come from? There must have been a cause which brought the universe into being. We can summarize our argument thus far as follows. Premise one, whatever begins to exist has a cause. Two, the universe began to exist. Three, therefore, the universe has a cause.

moves.description: Craig argues that an actually infinite past is impossible, astronomy confirms a cosmic beginning, and whatever begins to exist requires a cause.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig states a valid three-step causal syllogism and supports its second premise through both an argument against an actual infinite past and contemporary Big Bang cosmology. Principal limitation: Infinity-minus-infinity does not establish that actual infinities are contradictory, and the presentation moves too quickly from a cosmological boundary to absolute nothing while overstating what an atheist must accept. Live burden: Craig must defend temporal finitude, the interpretation of the astronomical evidence, and the qualified causal principle before any attributes of the cause can be inferred.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But the first argument is that the universe probably originated, my counter-argument is that the universe probably did originate by naturalistic means. After all, Big Bang, super strings theory and physics are, in fact, naturalistic theories that explain the origin of the universe. And they don't require, contrary to what Craig seems to think, as a default hypothesis, any other agency. But the point is that even if the universe were, in fact, created by a God, there would be no guarantee that there would be the particular Christian God that we're talking about here tonight. Any number of different gods would be able to make that kind of universe, and therefore this is really not an argument at all. It's completely irrelevant to the existence of the Christian God as much as it is relevant to a more general debate like the one that we had about three years ago in Tennessee.

moves.description: Pigliucci invokes Big Bang, superstring, and physical theories for a probable natural origin, then argues that creation would not uniquely identify the Christian God.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci gives a two-part reply, naming physical approaches that seek natural origins and correctly observing that even a creator conclusion would remain compatible with many non-Christian deities. Principal limitation: Merely citing Big Bang and superstring theory does not show that either explains an absolute origin or makes natural causation probable, and calling the argument irrelevant ignores its announced cumulative role. Live burden: His critical specificity point requires only showing underdetermination, while his positive claim of probable natural origin needs a model that actually engages Craig’s finite-past and causal premises.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Now by the very nature of the case, as the cause of space and time... This cause must be an uncaused, changeless, timeless, and immaterial being of unimaginable power which created the universe. Moreover, I would argue it must also be personal. For how else could a timeless cause give rise to a temporal effect like the universe? If the cause were an impersonal set of necessary and sufficient conditions, then the cause could never exist without the effect. If the cause were timelessly present, then the effect would be timelessly present as well. The only way for the cause to be timeless and for the effect to begin in time is for the cause to be a personal agent who freely chooses to create an effect in time without any prior determining conditions. And thus we are brought not merely to a transcendent cause of the universe, but to its personal creator.

moves.description: Craig contends that only a personal chooser can exist timelessly and freely initiate a temporal effect, making agency the best explanation of cosmic beginning.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig identifies a genuine explanatory pressure for any timeless cause: why an allegedly sufficient eternal condition does not yield an equally eternal effect, and he offers free agency as a direct answer. Principal limitation: Calling the cause a chooser labels the desired solution without independently demonstrating that timeless intention is coherent, causally intelligible, or more probable than unknown nonpersonal boundary conditions. Live burden: The affirmative must compare personal and impersonal explanations on common criteria and show that agency adds predictive or explanatory content rather than relocating the timing question inside an inscrutable will.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Now, the argument, of course, of the origin of the universe and where did it come from, I still don't understand. I talked to Dr. Craig several times before, and this might be, obviously, my personal limitation. But I don't understand how postulating a god actually solves anything. It seems to me that you fall into one of two traps. You either fall into an infinite regress, which he abhors. He said there's no infinity out there, because one can immediately ask, well, who created a god? How did a god come about? And then you say, well, there was super god. And how did super god come in? Well, there was super, super god, and obviously, he's gone forever. Or he becomes, all of a sudden, an Aristotelian, talking about a position that has been actually not following philosophy for thousands of years at this point. And he tells you that, well, there must have been an original cause that was uncaused. I'm not sure that that actually means anything outside of a philosophical mumbo jumbo. But it is interesting to see that actual quantum physicists have a very similar explanation, except that they can back it up with empirical evidence. They do actually have pretty good theories about how things literally come out of nothing.

moves.description: Pigliucci challenges God as an explanatory stopping point, invokes quantum uncertainty about causation, and warns that gaps in present knowledge do not establish supernatural agency.

Principal limitation: The regress objection partly misses Craig’s qualified premise about things that begin, quantum indeterminacy is not equivalent to uncaused existence from nothing, and scientific ignorance does not itself support a natural alternative. Live burden: He can weaken Craig’s necessity and agency inferences without producing a complete cosmology, but any positive quantum explanation must be specified and shown relevant to cosmic origins.

sourceSpan.excerpt: First consider the argument from the origin of the universe. Here we did get some argumentation now in the last speech. He says, quantum physics has shown that things can begin to exist without a cause. They can come out of nothing. That's a total misrepresentation. The quantum vacuum is not nothing. The quantum vacuum is a sea of fluctuating energy endowed with a rich physical structure and governed by physical laws. It is no exception to the principle that whatever begins to exist has a cause. Secondly, I pointed out the universe began to exist, and we've heard no refutation of this point tonight other than an attack on Fred Hoyle's credibility, but Stephen Hawking in his most recent book, The Nature of Space and Time, says today almost everyone believes that the universe and time itself had a beginning at the Big Bang. From those two premises it follows inescapably that therefore the universe had a cause, and all Dr. Piliucci does here is say, well, who created God? The answer is that for something that is timeless and eternal such as God must be, there is no cause. Whatever begins to exist has a cause is the relevant premise, but if something is timeless and eternal then it's impossible for it to come into being, so there isn't any cause for that. Of course, you can't say that about the universe anymore because the universe has shown to have had a beginning.

moves.description: Craig distinguishes the structured quantum vacuum from nothing and argues that God needs no cause because the causal premise applies only to entities that begin.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig makes two precise conceptual corrections: a quantum vacuum is a law-governed physical state rather than absolute nothing, and his causal premise does not say that every existing thing requires a cause. Principal limitation: These corrections defeat simplified objections but do not establish that the universe began from nothing, that a necessary personal being exists, or that every natural stopping point is inferior. Live burden: Craig must independently defend cosmic beginning, divine necessity, and the transition to agency, while Pigliucci should challenge those premises without equivocating over vacuum or universal causation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Quantum mechanics, we've been throwing quantum mechanics at each other tonight. And the interesting thing is that one of the best physicists who has ever worked on quantum mechanics, Richard Feynman, once said that if you think you understand quantum mechanics, you don't understand quantum mechanics. So there's a good chance that we're both wrong on quantum mechanics anyway. It would be nice to have a physicist in that. Is there a physicist in the hall? One. OK. One of my understandings of quantum mechanics, which, as I said, could be wrong, is, for example, that one of the major findings of quantum mechanics is exactly to put in question one of Dr. Craig's fundamental arguments, the causality, the cause-effect relationship. There are, in fact, under certain circumstances quantum phenomena that defy our understanding of cause and effect. And he says, well, the underlying quantum field is not nothing. It's pretty damn close to nothing. And especially because nobody understands what actually it is.

Principal limitation: Phenomena that defy present causal understanding are not thereby uncaused in Craig’s required sense, and calling the quantum field close to nothing supplies no clear physical or metaphysical criterion. Live burden: Pigliucci can challenge universalized ordinary causality without offering a replacement cosmology, but must identify a concrete quantum counterexample to move beyond disciplined uncertainty.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is due to design rather than physical law or chance.

moves.inference: Among law, chance, and design, the alleged exclusion of the first two leaves intelligent design as the explanation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: During the last 30 years, scientists have discovered that the existence and evolution of intelligent life depends upon a complex and delicate balance of initial conditions simply given in the Big Bang itself. We now know that life-prohibiting universes are vastly more probable than any life-permitting universe like ours. How much more probable? The answer is that the chances that the universe should be life-permitting are so infinitesimal as to be incomprehensible and incalculable. For example, Stephen Hawking has estimated that if the rate of the universe's expansion one second after the Big Bang had been smaller by even one part in a hundred thousand million million, the universe would have re-collapsed long ago into a hot fireball. P.C.W. Davies has calculated that the odds against the initial conditions being suitable for later star formation, without which planets couldn't exist, is one followed by a thousand billion billion zeros, at least. He also estimates that a change in the strength of gravity or of the weak force by even one part out of 10 to the 100th power would have prevented a life-permitting universe. There are around 50 constants and quantities in the Big Bang which must be fine-tuned in this way if the universe is to permit life. And it's not just each quantity that must be exquisitely fine-tuned. Their ratios to one another must also be fine-tuned. So improbability is added to improbability to improbability until our minds are reeling in incomprehensible numbers. There is no physical reason why these constants and quantities have the values they do. The one-time agnostic physicist Paul Davies comments, Through my scientific work, I have come to believe more and more strongly that the physical universe is put together with an ingenuity so astonishing that I cannot accept it merely as a brute fact. Similarly, Fred Hoyle remarks, A common-sense interpretation of the facts suggests that a super-intellect has monkeyed with physics. And Robert Jastrow, the head of NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies, has called this the most powerful evidence for the existence of God ever to come out of science. So once again, the view that theists have always held that there is an intelligent designer of the cosmos seems to make much more sense than the atheistic view that the universe, when it popped into being, uncaused, out of nothing, just happened to be, by chance, fine-tuned to an incomprehensible precision for the existence and evolution of intelligent life. We can summarize this second argument as follows. Premise one, the fine-tuning of the initial conditions of the universe is due to either law, chance, or design. Two, it is not due to law or chance. Three, therefore, it is due to design.

moves.description: Craig argues that life-permitting constants are highly improbable under chance or necessity, so intelligent design is the most plausible remaining explanation.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig presents fine-tuning as a comparative inference, distinguishing physical necessity, chance, and design and focusing attention on the narrow life-permitting range rather than merely expressing wonder at complexity. Principal limitation: The probability claims lack a justified distribution over possible constants, and the three-option menu is not shown to be exhaustive, so eliminating poorly specified rivals cannot by itself quantify design's likelihood. Live burden: He must justify the relevant possibility space, demonstrate that a designer would expect a life-permitting universe, and avoid using our existence as evidence without addressing selection effects.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The second point was that complexity of the universe. Well, the problem here is the same. It certainly is true that the universe is complex. It is also true that there are perfectly good naturalistic explanations for the complexity of the universe. There is an entire field of research that is called complexity theory of how things become more complex. And, of course, within biological organisms, there is the theory of evolution by natural selection that explains how organs can become more and more complex. But again, the problem is that's, by the way, that's a diagram of an eye to show you an example of complexity. But the point is, again, that any god would be able, by definition, to do or at least most versions of gods would be able to create a complex universe. After all, they are creators. And so that says absolutely nothing about the existence of the Christian God in particular, so we'll get rid of that argument as well.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci offers genuine examples of complexity increasing through natural processes and correctly notes that a complex creation would be compatible with numerous creator concepts rather than Christianity alone. Principal limitation: Complexity theory and biological evolution do not directly address Craig’s narrower claim about life-permitting constants and initial conditions, so the principal reply reconstructs fine-tuning as a different and easier target. Live burden: Pigliucci must engage why those parameters allegedly favor design, while his creator-nonuniqueness point appropriately preserves the separate demand for Christian specificity.

sourceSpan.excerpt: What about the argument from fine-tuning? The point is he's never been able to show how either law or chance could account for the fine-tuning of the initial conditions of the Big Bang, which point to an intelligent designer.

Live burden: Craig must supply positive comparative likelihood for design rather than inherit victory from unknown physics, while Pigliucci bears support for law or chance only insofar as he advances either as an actual explanation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: The fine tuning of the universe, which, again, is not really that relevant to discussion tonight, Dr. Craig was referring to the so-called entropic principle, the idea that the universe is so fine tuned, and the only explanation possible is that it was fine tuned to bring about this debate tonight, for example, which is a pretty twisted way of creating a universe, if you ask me. Now, he played the probability game. I don't have time to get into probability game. But a very good mathematician and probability theorist, Martin Gardner, actually went through these kind of games and defined the entropic principle as the completely ridiculous entropic principle, or CRAP for short. And so I'll leave it at that for the entropic principle. Incidentally, even if, and I'm not granted this at all, but even if science will never find out a satisfactory answer to the origin of the universe or to the origin of creation, or whatever you want to call it, that all amounts to say that we don't know. So what? Craig seems to think that he wins by default. You don't know, therefore. But it doesn't work that way. If we were having this debate 2,000 years ago, Dr. Craig would probably try to convince us all that lightning and thunder outside of the hole, which is not happening, would be an obvious indication of the fact that Zeus is upset. us and probably most of us would actually believe it because there was no theory of atmospheric physics at the time. So all he's making is an argument from ignorance and one of those things that science is very good at is debunking arguments from ignorance.

moves.description: Pigliucci declines Craig’s probability game, invokes Martin Gardner’s criticism, and argues that even permanent scientific ignorance would not make design win by default.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci clearly identifies a valid gap: failure to possess a present or future natural explanation would establish ignorance, not automatically supply positive evidence for an intentional designer. Principal limitation: He explicitly declines to analyze Craig’s probabilities, conflates the fine-tuning trilemma with an anthropic principle, and substitutes Gardner’s ridicule and a Zeus analogy for engagement with law, chance, or the numerical claims. Live burden: Pigliucci can block a default inference by exposing its form, but defeating the presented design case requires addressing its actual comparative warrant rather than treating all unresolved explanation as identical.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Objective moral values exist, and their existence entails God.
moves.warrant: Craig distinguishes moral knowledge from moral ontology, argues that evolutionary usefulness does not make acts really right or wrong, and appeals to judgments that rape, torture, child abuse, love, equality, and self-sacrifice have objective value.
moves.inference: Because objective values would not exist without God but do exist, God exists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage preserves the two-premise argument together with Craig's important clarification that atheists can know and practice morality; those qualifications prevent a misleading reconstruction despite the span's length.

sourceSpan.excerpt: If God does not exist, then objective moral values do not exist. Many theists and atheists alike concur on this point. For example, Michael Ruse, a noted philosopher of science, explains, the position of the modern evolutionist is that morality is a biological adaptation, no less than our hands and feet and teeth. Considered as a rationally justifiable set of claims about an objective something, ethics is illusory. I appreciate that when somebody says, love thy neighbor as thyself, they think they are referring above and beyond themselves. Nevertheless, such reference is truly without foundation. Morality is just an aid to survival and reproduction, and any deeper meaning is illusory. Friedrich Nietzsche, the great atheist who proclaimed the death of God, understood that the death of God meant the destruction of all meaning and value in life. I think that Friedrich Nietzsche was right. But we've got to be very careful here. The question here is not, must we believe in God in order to live moral lives? I'm not claiming that we must. Nor is the question, can we recognize objective moral values without believing in God? I certainly think that we can. Rather, the question is, if God does not exist, do objective moral values exist? Like Professor Roos, I just don't see any reason to think that in the absence of God, the herd morality evolved by Homo sapiens is objective. And here Dr. Piliucci agrees. He says, and I quote, I agree with Dr. Roos. There is no such thing as objective morality. Morality in human cultures has evolved, and what is moral for you might not be moral for the guy next door, and certainly is not moral for the guy across the ocean. On the atheistic view, some actions, say rape, may not be socially advantageous. And so in the course of human development, it has become taboo. But that does absolutely nothing to prove that rape is really wrong. On the atheistic view, there's nothing really wrong with your raping someone. Thus, without God, there is no absolute right and wrong that imposes itself on our conscience. But the problem is that objective values do exist, and deep down, I think we all know it. There's no more reason to deny the objective reality of moral values than the objective reality of the physical world. Actions like rape, torture, and child abuse aren't just socially unacceptable behavior. They're moral abominations. Professor Roos himself admits the man who says that it is morally acceptable to rape little children is just as wrong as the man who says 2 plus 2 equals 5. Some things, at least, are really wrong. Similarly, love, equality, self-sacrifice are really good. Thus, we can summarize this third argument as follows. Premise 1, if God does not exist, objective moral values do not exist. Premise 2, objective values do exist, from which it follows logically and inescapably. 3, therefore, God exists.

moves.description: Craig claims that objective moral values are apprehended in experience and require God as their ontological foundation, unlike evolutionary or social convention.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig separates the question of how moral beliefs arise from the question of what, if anything, makes moral claims objectively true, preventing an evolutionary genealogy from automatically dissolving normativity. Principal limitation: The inference from objective value to God is asserted more than demonstrated, because secular realism, reasons grounded in flourishing, or other accounts are not excluded merely by denying that adaptation creates obligation. Live burden: Craig must show why divine nature explains normativity without circularly presupposing goodness, while Pigliucci bears support only for the local or naturalistic objectivity he positively advances.

moves.inference: An evolved, context-sensitive account is a third option between divine universal morality and unrestricted relativism.

Selecting only the slogan would omit the empirical support he says demonstrates the account.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are objective but local truths
certain moral rules or certain decisions made by social animals are or are not adaptive
moves.attributionRationale: This is Pigliucci's uninterrupted opening argument.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the con's principal positive alternative to Craig's moral-grounding premise.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the premise that objective morality requires universality and divine grounding by proposing an evolved third option.

sourceSpan.excerpt: This is a direct quote from Dr. Craig. If God does not exist, then objective moral values do not exist. The problem is that objective values do exist, and deep down, we all know it. Yes, I agree that objective moral values exist, and I agree that we all know it deep down. The difference is that there is a distinction between objective values and universal moral values. And Dr. Craig seems to be talking about the two interchangeably, and I think that is a confusion of the two arguments. So let me present the first counter-argument. This is a false dichotomy. Essentially, what Dr. Craig is presenting is that he admits only two alternatives. Either there is a universal moral code, which is given to us by God, or anything goes, or there is only moral relativism. Well, this is definitely a false dichotomy, which in fact very few, if any, modern philosophers and ethicists fall for. There is a third option. In fact, there is a variety of third options. The third option is a family of options, and that is that there are objective but local truths. That is, there are some things that are objectively true, but they're only true under certain circumstances. For example, rape. He picked rape as an example for these arguments. Raping social animals is definitely wrong. It's objectively wrong. As Dr. Ruse said, quoted by Dr. Craig, it is objectively wrong because it just is not a good idea for social animals to allow people or members of their species to go around raping, or for that matter, killing other members of the same social group. You would not have a society in that case. So there is some objectivity to that. It is definitely objective that it's a bad idea to do it. There are animals, on the other hand, that use rape, for example, or what we would think of anthropomorphically as rape, as a way to gauge the strength of the male. And so the female actually battles with the male in order to determine if the male is good enough to inseminate her. Now, these things are pretty far from social animals like we conceive them. They're certainly not in the primate group. They are, for example, water striders. Now, for water striders, probably everybody would agree that morality doesn't even make any sense. It doesn't really apply. So there are some things that are moral, and are right, and are correct, they're truth, within certain boundaries. In this case, the social and biological boundaries of primates, not just human beings. And then, however, the same thing or similar behaviors just don't even pose the question under different circumstances, which is what I wanted to say in the quote that Dr. Craig actually brought up from me. The other counter-argument is that this is simply a non sequitur. Morality can come about without a God, and it can evolve by natural selection, because it is beneficial. So to state that if there are objective truths, that has to be. to imply that that's because they come from a god is simply not true. There are plenty of objective things that don't come from a supernatural being, and morality can be one of those. This can be demonstrated. This is not just simple talk. People have been working on these kinds of problems for the last few decades. And, for example, there are very sophisticated mathematical models based on game theory that show that, in fact, certain moral rules or certain decisions made by social animals are or are not adaptive, and therefore they are objectively better than others, and some others are objectively bad. This is something you can actually work on right now. There's also evidence consistent with my idea that, in fact, there are local moral truths, and this is empirical evidence that is brought up by the study of other primates. For example, our closest relatives, the pygmy chimpanzee or bonobos, they present behaviors that are, in several respects, very similar to the behavior of human beings. They do have moral rules, or what we would interpret as moral rules. They punish certain individuals for doing certain kinds of things, and those are the same kinds of actions that we don't allow in our society. So, not only it is morality, there are some aspects of morality, not all of it, that are objective for human beings, but, in fact, they are objective also for our cousins.

moves.description: Pigliucci defends objective but local moral truths grounded in human social life, arguing that universality across every conceivable being is unnecessary.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci offers a substantive middle position between divine command and crude relativism, locating objective moral assessment within shared human capacities, needs, and social conditions rather than personal preference. Principal limitation: Calling these truths objective and local leaves unclear whether their authority extends beyond contingent agreement, and the account does not fully explain why evolved dispositions generate reasons that bind agents who reject communal aims. Live burden: Because he positively proposes naturalized objectivity, he must articulate its truth-makers and normative force, while he need not ground duties for every possible creature or disprove all divine foundations.

But if you agree with me that the Holocaust was morally abominable, that it is really wrong to send people to gas chambers and concentration camps because of their Semitic origin, then you will agree with me that there is a transcendent basis in God for this. Now, Dr. Piliucci also says the Christian God is not moral, and he quotes several passages These are quoted out of context. sourceSpan.excerpt: Number 4, the historical facts concerning the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. The historical person, Jesus of Nazareth, was a remarkable individual. New Testament critics have reached something of a consensus that the historical Jesus came on the scene with an unprecedented sense of divine authority, the authority to stand and speak in God's place. He claimed that in himself the kingdom of God had come, and as visible demonstrations of this he carried out a ministry of miracle working and exorcisms. But the supreme confirmation of his claim was his resurrection from the dead. If Jesus did rise from the dead, then it would seem that we have a divine miracle. on our hands, and thus evidence for the existence of God. Now, most people would think that the resurrection of Jesus is something you just accept by faith or not. But there are actually three established historical facts recognized by the majority of New Testament historians today, which I believe are best explained by the resurrection of Jesus. Fact number one, on the Sunday following his crucifixion, Jesus' tomb was found empty by a group of his women followers. According to Jakob Kramer, an Austrian scholar who has specialized in the study of the resurrection, by far, most scholars hold firmly to the reliability of the biblical statements about the empty tomb. According to D.H. van Dahlen, it is extremely difficult to object to the empty tomb on historical grounds. Those who deny it do so on the basis of theological or philosophical assumptions. Fact number two, on separate occasions, different individuals and groups of people saw appearances of Jesus alive after his death. According to the prominent New Testament critic of Vanderbilt University, Gert Ludemann, it may be taken as historically certain that the disciples had experiences after Jesus' death in which Jesus appeared to them as the risen Christ. These appearances were witnessed not only by believers, but also by unbelievers, skeptics, and even enemies. Fact number three, the original disciples suddenly came to believe in the resurrection of Jesus despite having every predisposition to the contrary. You see, Jews had no belief in a dying, much less rising, Messiah. And Jewish beliefs about the afterlife precluded anybody's rising from the dead before the end of the world. Nevertheless, the original disciples suddenly came to believe so strongly that God had raised Jesus from the dead that they were willing to die for the truth of that belief. Luke Johnson, a New Testament scholar from Emory University, muses some sort of powerful, transformative experience is required to generate the sort of movement earliest Christianity was. N.T. Wright, an eminent British scholar, concludes that is why, as an historian, I cannot explain the rise of early Christianity unless Jesus rose again, leaving an empty tomb behind him. Attempts to explain away these three great facts, like the disciples stole the body or Jesus wasn't really dead, have been universally rejected by. temporary scholarship. The simple fact is that there just is no plausible, naturalistic explanation of these facts. Therefore, it seems to me the Christian is amply justified in believing that Jesus rose from the dead and was who he claimed to be. But that entails that God exists.

Live burden: Because this is the case’s principal Christian-specific bridge, Craig must defend the facts and compare resurrection with naturalistic and rival-religious explanations under equally demanding standards.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But first of all, the first counter-argument is that, in fact, there have been a multiplicity of messiahs all over the history of the human world, both before and after Jesus, and, in fact, at the same time as Jesus. So why would you pick one over another? There is little original, in fact, in the Christian religion. And historians and scholars of comparative religion will tell you that. The stories of the virgin birth, for example, the sacrifice, the resurrection, are found in a lot of previous cultures, including those that influence Hebraism and, therefore, Christianity. For example, Egyptians, Babylonians, and some Greek myth. And these are pretty well-documented. So Christians, like a lot of other religions before them, they just cut and paste, like you do in Windows, and put together new stories that are a slight variation on previous ones. Also, the moral precepts of Christianity are found, in fact, in other religions or philosophies. There's nothing particularly original about that either. And if you want an example, just go and read some of Plato's dialogues. Right there, there's Socrates, or what some people think Socrates looked like. And some passages in Socrates really do sound like Jesus talking to his disciples. The second argument was the empty tomb. Well, the problem with the empty tomb is that there are obvious explanations for these facts. I'm not really ready to acknowledge that these are facts. I think that these are speculations at best. Let's not forget that we're talking about events, alleged events, that occurred about 2,000 years ago, at which there were a few witnesses, and about which it was written several years after the actual events. So I'm not sure that these were actually facts. But let's grant for a minute that they were. Well, there are much easier explanations for each one of those facts that Dr. Craig brought up. For example, it is interesting that at the time, there was a practice of reburial of some criminals. Jesus was, of course, condemned by the Roman state as a criminal. And criminals were actually not even supposed to be buried if they were crucified. If they were, according to rabbinic law, they were buried in a common tomb. And so it's very possible that he was actually buried and then brought back to the final interration. Or there are simply many documented cases in history of mass hysteria. throughout the ages, up to the 20th century. And I don't really see much of a reason to invoke the supernatural if we can have a reasonable explanation within natural parameters.

sourceSpan.excerpt: So the resurrection, to put it as skeptic David Hume would have put it in the 18th century, is an extraordinary claim. Where is the extraordinary evidence? This is a very important point. There is nothing wrong with making extraordinary claims. And in fact, some of these extraordinary claims eventually do turn out to be correct. I mean, a physicist who tells you that you are made mostly of nothing is making a pretty extraordinary claim. Somebody tells you that this thing that looks and feels solid to me is actually made mostly of empty space. It's a pretty extraordinary claim. Fortunately for physicists, they back it up with powerful mathematical theories, which are also powerful backed up by empirical demonstrations. So I'm inclined to believe quantum mechanics when they tell me something about tables and physical bodies. But these kind of very extraordinary claims require a lot more evidence that Dr. Craig has been able to amass. There's also another counter-argument that I call the Elvis effect. There are far more people claiming that Elvis is alive and has resurrected and appears around in different places of the world than ever claim to have seen Jesus alive. Now, are we going to believe those people? And if not, you have to explain why not. It seems to me that on the surface, there's a lot more witnesses for that kind of event or, for example, for alien abductions or anything of the sort. In fact, Elvis actually does make miracles as well. This is a weeping Elvis miracle that you can find on the internet. You can purchase the picture, of course, as you like. And you can worship it. There's several religions, several cults about Elvis. Now, I'm being facetious here, but the question is, why would you not believe anything of this stuff unless you do believe that Elvis did? How many people here believe that Elvis is alive? Not that many. Good, because otherwise my argument would be much less effective. Oh, we found one. Now, the strength of belief argument, I don't think that proves absolutely anything. In fact, for one thing, most other religions can count on similar strength of convictions. Every member, well, maybe not every, but most members, most followers of most religions are actually characterized by very strong convictions. And in many cases, they're willing to die for it. We've seen examples in the 20th century pretty recently in the last few years. So does that make any kind of prediction about the fact that they were right? I mean, the people in the Heaven's Gate cult died because they thought that there was a UFO behind the comet. Does anybody believe that they were right and they're now happily basking around the universe opting on flying saucers? No, good. The Nazis believed very strongly and were willing to die by the hundreds of thousands to follow whatever that nutcase of Hitler was actually telling them to do. So obviously, being willing to die for a cause says absolutely nothing, unfortunately, about the truth of that cause.

Well, he compares them to Elvis sightings. Well, now look, Elvis sightings are typically explained in one of two ways. The resurrection appearances were clearly not lies because these people clearly believed in it. They were sincere. No Elvis-citer, I dare say, has been willing to go to a tortuous death in attestation of the belief that Elvis is risen from the dead. Neither can they be dismissed as hallucinations. Number one, the diversity of the appearances is too great. Secondly, hallucinations would not have led to believe in Jesus' resurrection, but at best, his assumption into heaven, not the resurrection of Jesus, which, as I explained, goes contrary to Jewish beliefs. Thirdly, it also leaves the empty tomb unexplained. Hallucinations does nothing to explain the empty tomb and is therefore an inadequate hypothesis. Thirdly, what about the origin of the disciples' belief? Here, he simply misconstrued the argument. It is not an argument based on the strength of their belief. And therefore, it cries out for some explanation of where this originated. Apart from the resurrection itself, I cannot find any antecedent cause that would explain why these people sincerely came to believe that Jesus was risen from the dead. So those are the facts, and I think that the best explanation of them is that they were telling the truth that Jesus was risen.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Okay, a few final words. It seems to me that Dr. Craig tried five arguments tonight, and I won't repeat them because we went both over them several times. The following conclusions seem reasonable to me. Three of these arguments do not apply to the existence of the Christian God, so he's missed the point entirely over there, and they're essentially irrelevant to our discussion tonight. If we wanted at the last minute to broaden this discussion to a more generalized kind of God, I'd be happy to do that. I've answered some of those arguments, but this was not what we were studying tonight. Those three arguments are no reason whatsoever to believe in the Christian God in particular. One argument, his last argument, is not even an argument by his own admission, so we can discard that one as well. So essentially, he's left here to talk to you for almost an hour, telling you to believe in miracles. That's his only argument. And I think that that's a pretty weak argument, especially because a lot of other religions can claim miracles. And they are equally convinced, as any Christian is, that their miracles are true, are correct, are empirically verifiable, are historically verifiable, and so on and so forth. So who is right? Are you sure you picked the right one? Miracles, the argument about miracles, has been debunked very thoroughly, much better than I could ever do, by David Hume back in the 18th century. And it's pretty surprising to me that people like Dr. Craig still use that kind of argument as their main defense of theism. I think the better thing you could do is simply to go out there and read Hume by yourself. It's not that difficult, and in fact, it's actually pretty entertaining. Now, he says, how about unicorns violate the laws of biology? So that's positive evidence that they don't exist. Well, by the same reason, you want to know a list of the laws of physics and biology that are violated by any religious claim to miracles? It's a long list. sourceSpan.excerpt: Finally, number five, the immediate experience of God. This isn't really an argument for God's existence. Rather, it's the claim that you can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments, simply by immediately experiencing him. This was the way people in the Bible knew God. As Professor John Hick explains, God was known to them as a dynamic will, interacting with their own wills, a sheer given reality, as inescapably to be reckoned with as destructive storm and life-giving sunshine. To them, God was not an idea adopted by the mind, but an experiential reality which gave significance to their lives. Now if this is the case, then there's a real danger that arguments for the existence of God could actually distract our attention from God himself. If you're sincerely seeking God, then God will make his existence evident to you. The Bible promises, draw near to God and he will draw near to you. We mustn't so concentrate on the external arguments that we fail to hear the inner voice of God speaking to our own hearts. For those who listen, God becomes an immediate reality in their lives.

But the point is, what does that prove other than a natural sense of awe? What does the feeling of awe and spiritual feeling with the universe, which I have and a lot of scientists that are non-believers do experience, that proves absolutely nothing. moves.speaker: Massimo Pigliucci
moves.claim: A brain-based hallucination is ordinarily a simpler and more reasonable explanation of hearing God than actual divine speech, without implying total skepticism or impossibility.
moves.warrant: Pigliucci affirms realism, invokes preference for significantly simpler explanations absent extraordinary contrary evidence, and explicitly allows that divine speech is possible.
moves.inference: Craig's external-world analogy overstates the challenge; comparative explanatory likelihood can defeat a particular religious experience without denying reality generally.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains Pigliucci's realism qualification, simplicity principle, worked religious-experience example, and fallibilist conclusion, ending before morality resumes.

moves.importanceRationale: It directly repairs the alleged skepticism consequence and states the con's comparative standard.

burdenContact.rationale: It frames hallucination as a more likely local explanation rather than a universal denial of experience.

sourceSpan.excerpt: He might mischaracterize quite a bit my hallucination argument. It did not point to a total skepticism. I'm certainly not a total skeptic. I'm way up there with philosopher Bertrand Russell, who once said that he will wish philosophers who don't believe in the existence of reality to get into a car and drive straight into a wall at a speed that is proportional to their belief that that wall is not there. So I'm definitely a realist from that perspective. My point was simply that there is a simpler explanation. And here, again, Dr. Craig doesn't seem to understand a basic tenet of not only scientific, but in fact, rational thinking. If there is a much simpler, significantly simpler explanation for a set of circumstances, you should go for that one first, unless there is extraordinary evidence that the alternative explanation is actually better. So if somebody tells you that, well, I just, oops, OK, I just hear God talking to me right now, it's much more likely that I'm having an hallucination than actually God is talking to me right at this moment. That doesn't mean that it's impossible that God is talking to me at this moment. Of course, if that were the case, I would immediately change, switch sides, and go on the other side of this debate. But the point is, it's a matter of what is reasonable. I said it right at the beginning of this debate that the point here is what is reasonable to understand and to believe, not what is true or not true. Neither Dr. Crank nor I actually have any foggy idea of what is true or not true, at least I don't, and I don't think he does either.

moves.description: Pigliucci affirms realism yet argues that hallucination ordinarily explains hearing God more simply than divine speech, which he expressly allows remains possible.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Pigliucci carefully separates local comparative explanation from total skepticism, affirms an external reality, and explicitly allows that God could be speaking while judging hallucination more reasonable absent extraordinary evidence. Principal limitation: Parsimony and familiar hallucinations are relevant, but he does not specify priors, case-specific evidence, or criteria for deciding when an experience’s content should overcome the simpler neural explanation. Live burden: He need only provide an independent defeater for uncorroborated experiential evidence, not prove divine speech impossible or undermine ordinary perception generally.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.claim: Brain systems and inducible hallucinations do not by themselves undermine religious experience any more than they undermine vision or hearing.
moves.warrant: Craig argues that sensory experience also depends on specialized brain regions and can be induced, yet remains trusted absent an independent defeater.
moves.inference: Pigliucci's neurological facts do not establish that Craig's experience is nonveridical.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span is the complete second-rebuttal restatement of the defeater argument, ending at Craig's turn boundary.

burdenContact.rationale: It clarifies why neurological mediation is not accepted as a sufficient defeater.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Dr. Piliucci did not come back on this. My point was that on his epistemology, it leads to utter skepticism because you can induce anything in the brain to hallucinate. The fact that there are portions of the brain that are geared toward religious experience no more undermines the veridicality of those experiences than the fact that there are portions of the brain geared for visual or auditory input undermines the veridicality of what you see and hear. He's got to give some independent defeater for thinking that my or Christian experience of God is non-veridical. And in the absence of any defeaters, and we haven't heard any tonight, there have been no reasons to falsify the hypothesis. There's simply no reason why I shouldn't trust my experience of God. He's real to me, and in the absence of a defeater of that, I'm perfectly rational in retaining that belief.

moves.description: Craig argues that neural mediation is compatible with genuine divine perception, just as ordinary sensory experience depends on brain processes without becoming illusory.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig correctly shows that discovering neural mediation does not logically settle whether an experience has an external object, since veridical perception ordinarily has measurable brain correlates. Principal limitation: The analogy establishes compatibility but not reliability, and religious experiences differ from ordinary perception in their conflicting interpretations, limited public access, and weak opportunities for independent checking. Live burden: Craig must identify features that make Christian experiences more trustworthy than induced or rival experiences if they are to add public evidence; Pigliucci need not infer falsehood from neural realization alone.
